---
title: "Smooth Morphisms"
subtitle: ""
---

A smooth morphism is the relative version of a nonsingular variety. Roughly, its fibers are smooth and fit together uniformly over the base.

::: {.callout-tip title="Mental picture"}
Think of a smooth morphism as a family of manifolds whose dimension stays constant and whose members do not suddenly acquire singularities.
:::

## Defitions
:::{#def-standard-smooth-morphism name="standard smooth morphism"}

The projection

$$
\operatorname{Spec}(R[x_1,\cdot, \cdot, x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\cdot, f_r)) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(R)
$$

is called the standard smooth morphism of relative dimension $n$ if the determinant of the matrix 

$$
\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}
$$

is invertible in the ring $R[x_1,\cdot, \cdot, x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\cdot, f_r)$. 
:::

:::{#rem-jacobson name=""}
The fibers of this morphism are smooth varieties of dimension $n$ by the Jacobian criterion. The condition on the determinant is a relative version of the Jacobian criterion.
:::

:::{#def-smooth-morphism name="smooth morphism"}
A morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ between schemes is **smooth** of relative dimension $n$ if there exist open subsets $\{U_i\}$ of $X$ and $\{V_i\}$ of $Y$ such that $\{U_i\}$ covers $X$ and $f(U_i)\subseteq V_i$ for each $i$, and the restriction $f|_{U_i}\colon U_i\to V_i$ is a standard smooth morphism of relative dimension $n$.
:::

:::{#rem-definition-of-smooth-morphism-slight-different name=""}
There are several equivalent variants of the definition of a standard smooth morphism that lead to the same notion of a smooth morphism.

1. We may allow a morphism which factors as
$$
U \hookrightarrow
\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\bigr)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Spec}(R),
$$
where the first morphism is an open immersion and the second morphism is standard smooth in the sense above.

2. We may replace the prescribed square Jacobian matrix by the full Jacobian matrix
$$
\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_
{\substack{1\leq i\leq r\\1\leq j\leq n+r}},
$$
and require that some $r\times r$ minor be invertible.

These variants give the same notion of a smooth morphism. If standard smoothness is defined as 1, we may assume $\{Y_i\}$ covers $Y$. One can combine 1 and 2 to weaken the standard smoothness again.
:::

::: {#rem-euiv-def name=""}
It is easy to show that we may define a smooth morphism by requiring that, for every $x\in X$, there exist an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ and an open neighborhood $V$ of $f(x)$ such that the induced morphism $f\colon U\to V$ is standard smooth. In this formulation, the full-rank condition may be weakened to the requirement that $df_1,\ldots,df_r$ be linearly independent in the fibre of $\Omega_{R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}]/R}$ at $x$.
:::

## Basic properties
::: {#prp-equivdef name=""}
A $k$-scheme is smooth of relative dimension $d$ over $k$, if it is of pure dimension $d$, and there exists a cover by affine open sets $\operatorname{Spec} k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ where the Jacobian matrix has corank $d$ at all points (not just closed points).
:::

:::{#prp-smooth-morphism-composition name=""}
If $f\colon X\to Y$ and $g\colon Y\to Z$ are smooth morphisms of relative dimension $n$ and $m$ respectively, then the composition $g\circ f\colon X\to Z$ is also smooth of relative dimension $n+m$.
:::
:::{.proof}
This is a local property, so we can assume that $f$ and $g$ are standard smooth morphisms of relative dimension $n$ and $m$ respectively. Then, by the chain rule, the corresponding Jacobian matrix of the composition $g\circ f$ is a block-upper-triangular matrix with the Jacobian matrices of $f$ and $g$ on the diagonal. Therefore, the determinant of the corresponding square matrix of $g\circ f$ is the product of determinants of the square matrices of $f$ and $g$, which are both invertible. So $g\circ f$ is a standard smooth morphism of relative dimension $n+m$.
:::

### Relation to differentials
We recall the definition and properties of the sheaf of differentials in [The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms](unramified-morphisms.qmd). The sheaf of differentials can be used to characterize smooth morphisms and smooth varieties.

:::{#prp-differentials-of-smooth-varieties name=""}
A scheme $X$ is smooth of relative dimension $n$ over $k$ if and only if the sheaf of differentials $\Omega_{X/k}$ is locally free of rank $n$ and $X$ is locally of finite type and of pure dimension $n$.
:::

:::{.proof}
Assume $X$ is smooth of relative dimension $n$. Then, by the relation between smoothness and regualrness, one can show that $X$ is reduced. Since $X$ is locally of finite type, the sheaf of differentials $\Omega_{X/k}$ is of finite type. By defineion, $X$ is locally standard smooth over $k$ of relative dimension $n$, we conclude that $\Omega_{X/k}|_x$ is free of rank $n$ for all $x\in X$. Thus, $\Omega_{X/k}$ is locally free of rank $n$. The other two conditions follow immediately from the definition of the smoothness.

Conversely, if $X$ satisfies the conditions, then since $\Omega_{X/k}$ is characterized by the cokernel of the Jacobian, the corank of the Jacobian must be $n$, which implies that $X$ is smooth of relative dimension $n$ by @prp-equivdef.
:::

:::{.callout-caution title="Caution"}
It is not easy to show that a smooth variety is reduced. The proof is not included here, but it can be found in the textbook "The Rising Sea". And the last statement in the proof above is a corollary of Nakayama's lemma, which is a fundamental result in alegbraic geometry, and both reducedness, finiteness and the constantness of the dimension of fibre matter. See 14.3.J in "The Rising Sea" for details.
:::

::: {#rem-smooth-free-differentials name=""}
When $f:X\to Y$ is a smooth morphism of relative dimension $n$, $\Omega_{X/Y}$ is locally free of rank $n$, since this is naturally true if $f$ is standard.
:::

::: {#prp-smooth-and-transitive-exact-sequence name=""}
Let $\pi\colon X\to Y$ and $\rho\colon Y\to Z$ be morphisms of schemes. If $\pi$ and $\rho$ are smooth, then the transitive exact sequence is also exact on the left, which means that the sequence
$$
0\to \pi^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\to \Omega_{X/Z}\to \Omega_{X/Y}\to 0
$$

is exact.
:::

:::{.proof}
This is a local property, so we can assume that $\pi$ and $\rho$ are standard smooth morphisms of relative dimension $n$ and $m$ respectively. In [The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms](unramified-morphisms.qmd), we know the module of differentials is the cokernel of the Jacobian matrix. The injectivity of the left follows from the fact that the Jacobian matrix of $\rho\circ \pi$ is a block-upper-triangular matrix with the Jacobian matrices of $\pi$ and $\rho$ on the diagonal.
:::

In the following, we will discuss the conormal exact sequence.

::: {#thm-conormal name=""}
Let $i:X\hookrightarrow Y$ be a closed immersion of smooth varieties over a field $k$, with ideal sheaf $\mathcal I$. Then the conormal sheaf
$$
\mathcal N^\vee_{X/Y}:=\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2
$$
is locally free, and the conormal sequence is a locally split short exact sequence
$$
0\longrightarrow \mathcal N^\vee_{X/Y}
\xrightarrow{\delta}i^*\Omega_{Y/k}
\longrightarrow\Omega_{X/k}
\longrightarrow 0,
$$
where $\delta(\overline f)=df|_X$.

Dualizing gives the normal exact sequence
$$
0\longrightarrow\mathcal T_{X/k}
\longrightarrow i^*\mathcal T_{Y/k}
\longrightarrow\mathcal N_{X/Y}
\longrightarrow 0,
$$
where $\mathcal N_{X/Y}:=(\mathcal N^\vee_{X/Y})^\vee$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Differentials and the conormal sheaf commute with field extension, while exactness and finite local freeness descend under faithfully flat base change. We may therefore assume that $k$ is algebraically closed.

Since $X$ and $Y$ are smooth over $k$, they are regular, and the closed immersion $i$ is a regular immersion. Thus $\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2$ is locally free of rank equal to the codimension of $X$ in $Y$.

The conormal sequence is always right exact:
$$
\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2
\xrightarrow{\delta}i^*\Omega_{Y/k}
\longrightarrow\Omega_{X/k}
\longrightarrow 0.
$$
Set $\mathcal K=\ker\delta$. Since $\mathcal K$ is a subsheaf of the locally free sheaf $\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2$, we have
$$
\operatorname{Ass}(\mathcal K)
\subseteq\operatorname{Ass}(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)
\subseteq\operatorname{Ass}(\mathcal O_X).
$$
As $X$ is reduced, its associated points are precisely the generic points of its irreducible components. Moreover, every nonzero coherent sheaf has an associated point. Hence it suffices to show that $\mathcal K_\eta=0$ at every generic point $\eta$ of $X$.

Fix such a point $\eta$, and work locally where $X$ and $Y$ have dimensions $m$ and $n$, respectively. Since $X$ is reduced, $\mathcal O_{X,\eta}=\kappa(\eta)$ is a field. Taking stalks gives a right-exact sequence of vector spaces
$$
(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)_\eta
\xrightarrow{\delta_\eta}(i^*\Omega_{Y/k})_\eta
\longrightarrow(\Omega_{X/k})_\eta
\longrightarrow 0.
$$
The dimensions of these three vector spaces are $n-m$, $n$, and $m$, respectively. Right exactness therefore gives
$$
\dim_{\kappa(\eta)}\operatorname{im}\delta_\eta=n-m
=\dim_{\kappa(\eta)}(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)_\eta.
$$
Thus $\delta_\eta$ is injective. It follows that $\mathcal K=0$, proving left exactness.

Since $\Omega_{X/k}$ is locally free, the resulting short exact sequence splits locally. Dualizing a locally split short exact sequence preserves exactness, giving the normal sequence.
:::

::: {#cor-cotangent-separable-closed-point name=""}
Let $Y$ be a smooth variety over a field $k$, and let $q\in Y$ be a closed point such that $\kappa(q)/k$ is separable. Write $\mathfrak m_q$ for the maximal ideal of $\mathcal O_{Y,q}$. Then the map
$$
\mathfrak m_q/\mathfrak m_q^2
\xrightarrow{\sim}
\Omega_{Y/k}\otimes_{\mathcal O_Y}\kappa(q),
\qquad
\overline f\longmapsto df\otimes 1,
$$
is a canonical isomorphism.
:::

::: {.proof}
The extension $\kappa(q)/k$ is finite separable, so $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(q)$ is smooth over $k$ and $\Omega_{\kappa(q)/k}=0$.
Applying the preceding theorem to the closed immersion
$\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(q)\hookrightarrow Y$ gives
$$
0\longrightarrow\mathfrak m_q/\mathfrak m_q^2
\longrightarrow\Omega_{Y/k}\otimes_{\mathcal O_Y}\kappa(q)
\longrightarrow\Omega_{\kappa(q)/k}
\longrightarrow 0.
$$
The last term vanishes, proving the first assertion.
:::

::: {.callout-note name=""}
The separability hypothesis is automatic when $k$ is perfect, in particular when $\operatorname{char}k=0$ or $k$ is finite. And the statement still holds when we do not require the smoothness of $Y$.
:::
